attrs.NOM_F: Zone de gestion de la faune de Kaskatamagan
attrs.LOCATION: 531,190  ha, east of the Nelson River on the Hudson Bay coast.
attrs.DESCRIPTION:
This WMA features a striking and abrupt transition from spruce forest to tundra along the edge of Hudson Bay. Protection of outstanding, yet fragile, coastal and tundra ecosystems led to the establishment of this WMA. This vast WMA includes habitat for polar bears, caribou and geese. Shorebirds are an important part of the fauna and plant life is a mix of arctic, sub-arctic, and boreal species. York Factory National Historic Site at the mouth of the Hayes River is adjacent to the WMA.

The fragile nature of the ecosystem and the potential hazards from wildlife and weather are reasons to visit this WMA through established lodges or tour operators.
attrs.GAME_SPP: Moose, Black Bear, Coastal or Barren-ground Caribou, Sharp-tailed Grouse, Ruffed Grouse, Spruce Grouse, Ptarmigan, Gray Wolf, Ducks, Geese, Sandhill Crane
attrs.HUNTING_RESTRICTIONS: No licenced caribou hunting between August 25 - September 30
attrs.Fur_spp: Beaver, Muskrat, Red Squirrel, Short-tailed Weasel, Marten, Mink, River Otter, Wolverine, Red Fox, Arctic Fox, Lynx

attrs.NOM_F: Zone de gestion de la faune de Narcisse
attrs.LOCATION: 11,882 ha, 5 km north of Narcisse on PTH 17, on the west side of the road
attrs.DESCRIPTION:
Narcisse WMA protects the largest aggregation of snakes in the world. To many, Narcisse is synonymous with snake. Its name even sounds like something a snake might say. The WMA is the winter denning grounds of tens of thousands of red-sided garter snakes.

The Narcisse WMA has become an international attraction and research station. Thousands of visitors come each year to see the snakes. Herpetologists have been studying the red-sided garter snake at Narcisse for more than 30 years. The researchers have made some interesting discoveries about snake physiology and behaviour. A good reason to study the red-sided garter snake is that it isn't venomous.

The many research projects have helped to protect the snakes. One example is the small snake fences you will notice along the PTH #17 – they channel the snakes to culverts under the road. In past snakes were killed in the thousands on the road during spring and fall migration.

Why here is often asked. The karst topography of the Interlake allows the snakes to survive our harsh winters. The limestone bedrock is full of cracks, crevices and caverns. Over thousands of years a weak acid, made of water and carbon dioxide, has percolated through the soil to the limestone bedrock, dissolving it to form the caverns below the frost line but above the water table – a safe place for the snakes to wait out the winter. Another factor is that the snakes' summer habitat is also protected by the surrounding WMAs.

You can visit year round – Narcisse WMA is more than snakes. The WMA also protects critical winter habitat for deer. Watch for coyote, red fox and snowshoe hare. Some of the avian life you can see include ruffed and sharp-tailed grouse, eastern bluebird, veery, warbling vireo, brown thrasher, vesper sparrow, Cape May warbler, Connecticut warbler, northern harrier and other raptors.

The ideal times to see the snakes are in the spring (early May), when the snakes are first emerging from their winter hibernacula, or the fall, when they are returning to their underground dens for the winter. There are four den sites to visit on a well-marked trail. You will find interpretive signs throughout.

In addition to the interpretive trail that takes you around to the dens, the Old Pioneer Trail cuts through the Narcisse WMA on its way from Grosse Isle up to Fisher Branch. The Old Pioneer Trail is a great biking trail that takes you through the Inwood, Sandridge and Narcisse WMAs. It also passes close to the Clematis and Broad Valley WMAs. It is unlawful to kill, harass or remove any snakes from the WMA. Call the TIP line at 1-800-782-0076 if you see something that should be reported to wildlife officials.
